note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 53-year-old male here for follow-up of your psoriatic arthritis. How have things been since we last met?
Patient: Not great. The joint pain in my hands is back, and my right second toe has been swollen and sore for about six weeks. Mornings are the worst, I have stiffness for almost an hour.
Doctor: Any back pain, or pain in your heels?
Patient: My right heel hurts when I first get out of bed, but no back pain.
Doctor: Any red or painful eyes, or blurry vision?
Patient: No, my eyes are fine.
Doctor: How about fever, diarrhea, or belly pain?
Patient: No fever, no diarrhea, and no belly pain.
Doctor: And the skin?
Patient: I still get scaly patches on both elbows and my scalp, but they are not any worse.
Doctor: Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take methotrexate 15 mg once a week and folic acid 1 mg every day. I also take naproxen 500 mg twice a day for the joint pain, which is most days now. For my blood pressure I take amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Doctor: Any alcohol with the methotrexate?
Patient: Just one beer on weekends.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are blood pressure 134 over 84, heart rate 76, and temperature 36.8 Celsius. On exam your right second toe is swollen and sausage-like, three finger joints in your right hand are tender and swollen, you have tenderness where the right Achilles tendon attaches, there is nail pitting, and you have scaly plaques on both elbows. Your knees and shoulders look fine. Your labs from last week show an ESR of 32 and a CRP of 18 mg/L, while your ALT and creatinine were normal. The hand X-rays show no erosions.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: You have active psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and enthesitis despite the methotrexate, plus plaque psoriasis and well-controlled hypertension. I would like to add adalimumab 40 mg injected under the skin every other week. Before the first dose we need a TB test and hepatitis screening, so I am ordering a QuantiFERON and hepatitis B and C blood tests today. Continue methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid. Once the injections are working, we can cut the naproxen down. Come back in 12 weeks, and call us right away if you get a fever or any infection.
Patient: Can I give the injection myself?
Doctor: Yes, our nurse will teach you. Please wait for the TB result before the first injection.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 53-year-old male with psoriatic arthritis came in for follow-up with recurrent hand joint pain, a swollen and sore right second toe for about six weeks, and nearly an hour of morning stiffness. He denied back pain, eye symptoms, fever, diarrhea and belly pain. Exam showed a sausage-like right toe, tender and swollen finger joints, Achilles tenderness, nail pitting and elbow plaques, with an ESR of 32, CRP of 18 mg/L and no erosions on hand X-rays. The assessment was active psoriatic arthritis despite methotrexate, with plaque psoriasis and well-controlled hypertension. Adalimumab 40 mg every other week will be added after TB and hepatitis screening, with follow-up in 12 weeks.

The right heel hurts when first getting out of bed. Denies back pain, red or painful eyes, blurry vision, fever, diarrhea and belly pain. Scaly patches on both elbows and the scalp are not any worse. Takes methotrexate 15 mg once a week, folic acid 1 mg every day, naproxen 500 mg twice a day (most days now) and amlodipine 5 mg daily. One beer on weekends.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 134 over 84, heart rate 76, temperature 36.8 Celsius. Right second toe swollen and sausage-like, three finger joints of the right hand tender and swollen, tenderness where the right Achilles tendon attaches, nail pitting, and scaly plaques on both elbows. Knees and shoulders look fine. ESR 32, CRP 18 mg/L, ALT and creatinine normal. Hand X-rays show no erosions.
soap.assessment: Active psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and enthesitis despite methotrexate, plaque psoriasis, and well-controlled hypertension.

Order QuantiFERON and hepatitis B and C blood tests before the first injection, and wait for the TB result

note:
Doctor: Hello, thanks for coming in. I have you down as a 67-year-old female with burning when you urinate. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: It started two days ago. It burns every time I pee, I am running to the bathroom all the time, and my lower belly aches. This is the fourth infection since last winter, and I am so tired of this.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever and no chills.
Doctor: Any pain in your back or sides, nausea, or vomiting?
Patient: No back pain, no nausea, no vomiting.
Doctor: Have you seen any blood in your urine?
Patient: No, I have not seen any.
Doctor: What did they treat the earlier infections with?
Patient: Twice with ciprofloxacin, and once with nitrofurantoin. The last culture grew E. coli.
Doctor: Do you leak urine, or have trouble emptying your bladder?
Patient: I leak a little when I cough, but I empty fine.
Doctor: Any vaginal dryness or discomfort since menopause?
Patient: Yes, I have been dry for years and it is uncomfortable.
Doctor: What other health problems do you have, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: High blood pressure and high cholesterol. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning and atorvastatin 40 mg at night.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: A pack a day for about 40 years. I know, I know.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 142/86, heart rate 78, temperature 37.0 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Your lower belly is tender just above the pubic bone, but there is no tenderness over your flanks. The urine dipstick is positive for leukocytes and nitrites, with a trace of blood. I also did a bladder scan, and you are emptying well, with only 40 mL left after you void.
Patient: So is it another infection?
Doctor: Yes, you have an acute bladder infection, and with four in a year this is recurrent UTI. The dryness after menopause is likely contributing. Smoking also raises the risk of bladder cancer, so we need to look at your urinary tract. Here is the plan. I am starting nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice a day for five days and sending a urine culture. I am also starting estradiol vaginal cream 0.5 g twice a week at bedtime to help prevent future infections. I am ordering a renal and bladder ultrasound and referring you for cystoscopy because of your smoking history and the repeated infections. I would also like you to quit smoking, so let us start a nicotine patch 21 mg daily, and I will give you the quit line information.
Patient: Okay, I will give the patch a try.
Doctor: Come back to the emergency department if you get a fever, back pain, or vomiting. Follow up in the urology clinic in four weeks.
summary: A 67-year-old female smoker presented to urgent care with two days of burning urination, urinary frequency and lower belly aching, her fourth urinary infection since last winter. She denied fever, chills, back pain, nausea, vomiting and visible blood in the urine. Her urine dipstick was positive for leukocytes and nitrites, and a bladder scan showed 40 mL left after voiding. The assessment was an acute bladder infection with recurrent UTI, with postmenopausal vaginal dryness as a likely contributor. Nitrofurantoin, estradiol vaginal cream and a nicotine patch were started, with a urine culture, renal and bladder ultrasound, cystoscopy referral and urology follow-up in four weeks.

soap.subjective: Two days of burning with urination, urinary frequency and lower belly aching, the fourth infection since last winter. Denies fever, chills, back pain, nausea, vomiting and blood in the urine. Earlier infections were treated twice with ciprofloxacin and once with nitrofurantoin, and the last culture grew E. coli. Leaks a little when she coughs but empties fine; vaginal dryness for years since menopause. History of high blood pressure and high cholesterol, taking amlodipine 5 mg every morning and atorvastatin 40 mg at night. Smokes a pack a day for about 40 years.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 142/86, heart rate 78, temperature 37.0 Celsius, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lower belly tender just above the pubic bone with no tenderness over the flanks. Urine dipstick positive for leukocytes and nitrites with a trace of blood. Bladder scan shows 40 mL left after voiding.
soap.assessment: Acute bladder infection in the setting of recurrent UTI, with postmenopausal dryness likely contributing; smoking history raises concern for urinary tract pathology.

note:
Visit type: Telehealth video visit (synchronous audio and video), psychiatry follow-up. The patient connected from home in a private room and consented to telehealth, and her location and identity were confirmed verbally. A professional Spanish medical interpreter joined by video for the entire visit, and no family member interpreted.

Reason for visit: Six-week follow-up of generalized anxiety disorder in a 31-year-old female.

Interval history (patient-reported through the interpreter): She started sertraline 50 mg every morning six weeks ago. Mild nausea in the first two weeks has resolved, and she has missed two doses in total. She still worries excessively most days about work and her children, and she has muscle tension in her neck and shoulders, trouble falling asleep about four nights a week, and irritability. She uses hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed about three nights a week, with some benefit for sleep. She drinks three cups of coffee a day. She denies panic attacks, chest pain, and palpitations. She denies depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and thoughts of self-harm. She does not use alcohol or drugs.

Home measurements: Blood pressure 118/74 and pulse 82 on her home cuff this morning. Weight was not measured.

Limited video exam: Well groomed and comfortable on camera, in no acute distress. Speech is normal in rate and volume. Mood described as anxious, with a mildly anxious but congruent affect. Thought process is linear. No visible tremor or psychomotor agitation. No hallucinations or delusions expressed. Insight and judgment are good.

Data: GAD-7 score today is 14, down from 18 at baseline. PHQ-9 score is 6. TSH was 1.9 at the baseline workup.

Impression: Generalized anxiety disorder with a partial response to sertraline 50 mg after six weeks, tolerating the medication well. Caffeine intake is likely contributing to the sleep difficulty and muscle tension.

Treatment and follow-up: Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg every morning. Continue hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed. Reduce coffee to one cup a day and review sleep hygiene. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy with a Spanish-speaking therapist. Reviewed sertraline side effects and when to seek care. Safety plan reviewed and the 988 crisis line provided. Repeat GAD-7 at the next visit. Follow-up telehealth video visit in four weeks, with a professional interpreter booked in advance.
summary: A 31-year-old female with generalized anxiety disorder was seen by video with a professional Spanish interpreter for six-week follow-up on sertraline 50 mg. She still has excessive worry, muscle tension, trouble falling asleep and irritability, and denies panic attacks, depressed mood and suicidal ideation. Her GAD-7 score was 14, down from 18, and the video exam showed a mildly anxious but congruent affect with linear thought process. The impression was generalized anxiety disorder with partial response to sertraline and caffeine contributing to sleep difficulty. Sertraline was increased to 100 mg every morning, and cognitive behavioral therapy referral, caffeine reduction and a four-week video follow-up were arranged.

Denies panic attacks, chest pain, palpitations, depressed mood, suicidal ideation and thoughts of self-harm. Does not use alcohol or drugs.

Video exam: well groomed, comfortable and in no acute distress, normal speech, anxious mood with a mildly anxious but congruent affect, linear thought process, no visible tremor or psychomotor agitation, no hallucinations or delusions expressed, good insight and judgment. GAD-7 score 14 (18 at baseline), PHQ-9 score 6, TSH 1.9 at the baseline workup.

Continue hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed

K was 6.4 and Cr 2.6 from a baseline of 1.9, and the ECG showed peaked T waves that improved after calcium gluconate, insulin with D50, albuterol and Lokelma. The impression was hyperkalemia from supplements, a salt substitute and an ACEi in the setting of AKI on CKD 3b. The supplements and ibuprofen were stopped, lisinopril was held, and he was admitted to telemetry observation with nephrology following.

note:
Doctor: Hi, I have you down as a 43-year-old female with heartburn that is not getting better. What has been going on?
Patient: I have had burning in my chest, right behind the breastbone, almost every day for about a year. It gets worse after dinner and when I lie down, and sometimes I taste acid in my throat.
Doctor: What are you taking for it?
Patient: Omeprazole 20 mg once a day for the last three months. It helped a little at first, but now I am back to the same symptoms. I also chew antacids when it gets bad.
Doctor: When do you take the omeprazole?
Patient: Usually with my coffee in the morning, right before breakfast.
Doctor: Good. Any trouble swallowing, vomiting, or black stools?
Patient: No trouble swallowing, no vomiting, and no black stools.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: No, my weight is stable.
Doctor: Any chest pain with exertion or shortness of breath?
Patient: No, it is just the burning, and it goes away with the antacids sometimes.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 118/72 and your heart rate is 70. Your belly is soft with mild tenderness in the upper middle part, and there is no guarding. I think you have refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease, since the once-a-day omeprazole is not controlling it. I am going to increase your omeprazole to 40 mg twice a day, taken 30 minutes before breakfast and dinner. I would also like to schedule an upper endoscopy to look at the esophagus and take biopsies if needed. Please avoid eating within three hours of bedtime and raise the head of your bed.
Patient: How long should I stay on the higher dose?
Doctor: Eight weeks, and then we will reassess at your follow-up visit after the endoscopy. Go to the emergency department if you have trouble swallowing, vomit blood, or have black stools.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 43-year-old female presented to urgent care with burning behind the breastbone almost daily for about a year, worse after dinner and when lying down, with an acid taste in the throat. She has not improved on omeprazole 20 mg once a day for three months and denied trouble swallowing, vomiting, black stools, weight loss, exertional chest pain and shortness of breath. Examination showed a soft abdomen with mild upper middle tenderness and no guarding. The assessment was refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease. Omeprazole was increased to 40 mg twice a day for eight weeks, an upper endoscopy was planned, and bedtime and head-of-bed measures were advised.

Go to the emergency department for trouble swallowing, vomiting blood or black stools

Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 60-year-old male here for follow-up of your interstitial lung disease. How have your breathing and cough been?
Patient: Worse, honestly. I get winded just walking to the mailbox now, and I have this dry cough that never goes away.
Doctor: How long has the shortness of breath been getting worse?
Patient: About four months. It used to be only on the stairs.
Doctor: Any fever, coughing up blood, or chest pain?
Patient: No fever, no blood, and no chest pain.
Doctor: Any leg swelling or wheezing?
Patient: No swelling in my legs, and no wheezing that I notice.
Doctor: How is your acid reflux, and what do you take for it?
Patient: Fine on the pantoprazole 40 mg every morning. I also take lisinopril 10 mg daily for my blood pressure.
Doctor: Do you still smoke?
Patient: No, I quit about ten years ago.
Doctor: Tell me about your home situation.
Patient: I live alone. My brother lives two states away, so there is nobody around to help if something goes wrong, and I worry about managing all of this by myself.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. We will build some support into the plan. Now, your vitals today: BP 128/78, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air at rest. When you walked the hallway for six minutes your saturation dropped to 87%. On exam you have fine crackles at both lung bases and mild clubbing of the fingers, with no leg edema. Your breathing test from last week shows an FVC of 68% of predicted, down from 76% six months ago, and a DLCO of 44% of predicted. Your high-resolution CT shows basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, which is a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: It means you have fibrotic interstitial lung disease that is progressing, most consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. I would like to start nintedanib 150 mg twice a day to slow the scarring. It can cause diarrhea and liver test changes, so I am ordering liver function tests today and then monthly for three months. Because your oxygen drops with activity, I am also prescribing supplemental oxygen at 2 liters per minute with exertion. Continue the pantoprazole and lisinopril. I am referring you to pulmonary rehab and to our social worker, and I am arranging a home health nurse to set up the oxygen equipment and teach you how to use it, since you live alone.
Patient: I can give you my brother's contact information for emergencies.
Doctor: Good, please do that. Follow up with me in six weeks. Call us sooner if your breathing suddenly gets worse, or if you have a fever or cough up blood.
Patient: Okay, thank you.

Doctor: Welcome back. I have you down as a 61-year-old female here for follow-up of the blood clot in your left leg. You are about six months into treatment, correct?
Patient: Yes, that is right.
Doctor: How is the leg?
Patient: Much better. There is only a little swelling by the end of the day.
Doctor: Any new pain in the calf, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
Patient: No pain in the calf, no chest pain, no trouble breathing.
Doctor: What blood thinner are you taking, and how are you taking it?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day. But I work rotating shifts at a distribution center, some weeks nights and some weeks days, so the timing is all over the place. I miss a dose about once a week.
Doctor: I appreciate your honesty. Any bleeding, like nosebleeds, bleeding gums, black or bloody stools, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No nosebleeds, no bleeding gums, no black stools, and no blood in my urine. I just have a couple of small bruises.
Doctor: Any other pills, including over-the-counter ones?
Patient: Atorvastatin 20 mg at night, and ibuprofen 400 mg a couple of times a week for my knees.
Doctor: Okay, we need to talk about the ibuprofen. Your vitals today are BP 126/78, HR 74, SpO2 98% on room air, and weight 78 kg. Your left calf is slightly swollen compared with the right, soft, and not tender. The ultrasound of your leg veins today shows the clot in the left popliteal vein is mostly dissolved, with a small amount of residual nonocclusive thrombus. Your blood count is normal with hemoglobin 12.8 and platelets 245, and your creatinine is 0.9. Your mammogram and colonoscopy are up to date, and nothing suggests a hidden cancer.
Patient: So what happens now?
Doctor: This was an unprovoked DVT with no clear trigger, so the risk of it coming back is higher. After six months, I recommend staying on a blood thinner long term but at a lower dose, so I am reducing your apixaban from 5 mg twice a day to 2.5 mg twice a day. I am also stopping the ibuprofen, because with a blood thinner it raises your bleeding risk. You can use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for your knees instead.
Patient: My schedule is the hard part. What should I do with the shifts?
Doctor: Count your day from when you wake up, whether that is morning or evening. Take one dose when you wake and the second dose about 12 hours later, set two phone alarms that move with your shift, and use a weekly pill box. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day, and do not double up.
Patient: That makes sense. I can do that.
Doctor: Good. Come back in three months with a CBC and a creatinine check. Go to the emergency department right away for new chest pain, trouble breathing, a swollen painful leg, black stools, or bleeding that will not stop.

Doctor: Welcome back. I have you down as a 30-year-old female here for your week four visit for the infection in your right shin bone, the osteomyelitis. How have you been?
Patient: Honestly, tired, but the leg is better. The pain is down to a dull ache and the swelling is mostly gone.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?
Patient: No fever, no chills, no night sweats.
Doctor: Any drainage or redness at the surgical scar?

Doctor: How about the PICC line in your left arm? Any pain, redness, or swelling there?

Doctor: Let us go over how you have been giving the cefazolin. It is supposed to be 2 grams every 8 hours through the PICC.
Patient: I do it every 8 hours, like they taught me.
Doctor: Is that really the case, with your work schedule?
Patient: Actually, no, I should be honest. I work rotating shifts at a distribution center, and on workdays I only manage the morning dose and the late night dose. I skip the middle one most days, so on workdays I get two doses, and on my days off I get all three.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, that is really important. What other medicines do you take?
Patient: Levothyroxine 100 mcg every morning, a fluticasone inhaler two puffs twice a day and albuterol two puffs as needed for my asthma, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day for my iron deficiency anemia, and acetaminophen 650 mg as needed for the leg. I stopped the ibuprofen two weeks ago.
Doctor: Good. Now your vitals: BP 112/70, HR 78, temperature 36.9 Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air. The surgical scar over your right shin is healed with no redness, warmth, or drainage, and there is mild tenderness over the distal tibia. The PICC site is clean and dry, your lungs are clear with no wheezing, and I do not see a rash. Your labs this week show a white count of 7.8, hemoglobin 11.4, platelets 392, and creatinine 0.7, and your ALT is normal. Your ESR is 48, down from 96, and your CRP is 1.8, down from 9.6. Your TSH is 6.8, which is high for someone with hypothyroidism on treatment. The MRI of your right tibia last week shows improving marrow edema and no abscess. The bone culture from your surgery grew MSSA, which is sensitive to both cefazolin and ceftriaxone.
Patient: So am I getting better?
Doctor: Yes, you have improving MSSA osteomyelitis, even with the missed doses, and your asthma and anemia look stable. But the every-8-hour schedule does not fit your life, so I am stopping the cefazolin and starting ceftriaxone 2 grams once daily through the PICC, which is just as effective for this organism. You can give it at the same time each day, right after you finish your shift or before you go to sleep. A home infusion nurse will teach you and deliver the supplies. We will finish the full six weeks, so two more weeks. I am also increasing your levothyroxine from 100 mcg to 112 mcg every morning, and we will recheck the TSH in six weeks. Continue the fluticasone, albuterol, ferrous sulfate, and acetaminophen. We will check a CBC with differential, creatinine, ALT, ESR, and CRP weekly, and your home nurse will change the PICC dressing weekly.

Doctor: Call us for fever, new redness, pain or swelling at the PICC or in your arm, severe diarrhea, or a rash. Come back in two weeks for your end of treatment visit.
Patient: Okay, I will set an alarm for the new schedule.

HPI: 18-year-old female with antiphospholipid syndrome and a prior left leg DVT, on warfarin 5 mg daily, who presents with a sudden, severe headache that began about 2 hours before arrival while she was sitting at her desk at school. Pain reached maximal intensity within seconds, is diffuse, and is 9/10. She describes it as the worst headache of her life. She has associated nausea and photophobia. She denies head trauma, falls, fever, neck stiffness, vision loss, double vision, focal weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, and seizure. She has had milder headaches with nausea in the past that improved with sleep. She took her last warfarin dose last night and reports no missed doses. No new medications or recent illness.

ROS:
Constitutional: Negative for fever and chills.
Eyes: Positive for photophobia. Negative for vision loss and double vision.
GI: Positive for nausea. Negative for vomiting.
Neurologic: Positive for headache. Negative for focal weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, and seizure.

Physical Exam:
Vitals: BP 124/76, HR 88, RR 16, Temp 37.0 C, SpO2 99% on room air.
General: Uncomfortable, lying in a dim room, alert.
HEENT: Atraumatic, no scalp hematoma, pupils equal and reactive, no papilledema.

Neuro: Alert and oriented, cranial nerves II-XII intact, strength 5/5 in all extremities, sensation intact, no pronator drift, normal finger-to-nose and gait.

Treated with 1 L normal saline IV, metoclopramide 10 mg IV, diphenhydramine 25 mg IV, and acetaminophen 1000 mg PO. Headache improved from 9/10 to 3/10 over 2 hours. NSAIDs were avoided because of warfarin.

Medical Decision Making: 18-year-old on therapeutic warfarin (INR 2.6) with a thunderclap-type headache, so subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis were the main concerns given her antiphospholipid syndrome. CT within 6 hours of onset was normal per neuroradiology, which effectively excludes subarachnoid hemorrhage, and CT angiography and venography were negative. No fever or meningismus, so meningitis is unlikely, and lumbar puncture was deferred given anticoagulation and the negative workup. Her headache responded to migraine therapy, and the final diagnosis is migraine without aura. INR is therapeutic and no reversal is needed.

Disposition: Discharged home with a parent after observation. Continue warfarin 5 mg daily with an INR recheck in 1 week through the anticoagulation clinic. Acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed for headache; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Neurology follow-up in 2 weeks. note:
Doctor: Hello, I am the emergency doctor. I have you down as an 81-year-old female with a cut on your arm. What happened?
Patient: I was reaching into the kitchen cabinet and a glass jar slipped and broke, and a piece cut my left forearm. It happened about an hour ago.
Doctor: Did you fall, hit your head, or pass out?
Patient: No, I did not fall, I did not hit my head, and I did not pass out.
Doctor: Any numbness, tingling, or trouble moving your fingers?
Patient: No numbness and no tingling, and I can move all my fingers.
Doctor: Are you on any blood thinners, and when was your last tetanus shot?
Patient: No blood thinners. I take acetaminophen 500 mg when my arthritis flares up, and my last tetanus shot was three years ago.
Doctor: Good, so your tetanus is up to date. Let me look. Your blood pressure is 138/80 and your heart rate is 76. You have a clean, 4 cm straight laceration on the inner side of your left forearm. The bleeding has stopped with pressure. After rinsing it out I do not see any glass in the wound, and you have full finger and wrist movement, normal sensation, and good circulation in your hand. The tendons look intact. I am also going to get a quick X-ray to make sure no glass is left behind.
Patient: Will I need stitches?
Doctor: Yes, it is deep enough that it needs closure. The X-ray is clear with no glass. I will numb the area with lidocaine 1% and close it with five stitches.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: All done, the wound is closed. Keep it clean and dry for 48 hours, then you can wash it gently. You can take acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. Watch for redness, swelling, pus, or fever. Your stitches come out in 10 days at your primary care office.
Patient: Thank you, doctor.
summary: An 81-year-old female presented to the ED about an hour after a broken glass jar cut her left forearm, and she denied falling, hitting her head, passing out, numbness and tingling. She takes acetaminophen for arthritis, is not on blood thinners, and her last tetanus shot was three years ago. Exam showed a clean 4 cm straight laceration with bleeding controlled, intact tendons, full movement, normal sensation and good circulation, and an X-ray showed no retained glass. The wound was numbed with lidocaine 1% and closed with five stitches. She was told to keep it clean and dry for 48 hours, take acetaminophen as needed, watch for infection, and have the stitches removed in 10 days.

note: Dictation for a gastroenterology clinic visit. This is a 40-year-old female referred for progressive difficulty swallowing. She reports about four months of food sticking in the lower chest when she swallows solids like meat and bread, and it has progressed so that she now has trouble with soft foods like rice and pasta as well, but liquids go down fine. She has also had weight loss of about 6 pounds over this time. She has a long history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and takes omeprazole 40 mg, correction, that should be 20 mg once daily, with only partial relief of the heartburn. She denies painful swallowing, denies vomiting blood, denies black stools, denies hoarseness, and denies chest pain. She is a nonsmoker and drinks alcohol rarely. On exam blood pressure is 120 over 76, heart rate 72, weight 62 kilograms, and the abdomen is soft and nontender with no masses. Impression is progressive solid food dysphagia, most likely from a peptic esophageal stricture related to her long-standing reflux, with eosinophilic esophagitis and esophageal malignancy also in the differential given the weight loss. Plan is to schedule an upper endoscopy with biopsies within two weeks, with dilation if a stricture is found, and to continue omeprazole 20 mg once daily for now. I advised her to eat small soft meals, chew thoroughly, and sit upright after meals, and to go to the emergency department if she cannot swallow liquids or saliva. Follow up in clinic after the endoscopy.

Her abdominal exam was soft and nontender with no masses. The impression was progressive solid food dysphagia, most likely from a peptic esophageal stricture. An upper endoscopy with biopsies and possible dilation was planned within two weeks, omeprazole continues, and she received swallowing and return precautions.
